COMPUTER FRAUD AND ABUSE ACT CIVIL REMEDY — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

WHAT THIS INFORMATION SHEET COVERS
This information sheet describes the private civil remedy in the federal Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA), 18 U.S.C. section 1030(g). Section 1030(g) lets a person who suffers damage or loss from certain violations of section 1030 bring a civil lawsuit against the violator. It covers which kinds of violations qualify for a civil suit, the $5,000 aggregate-loss factor most often relied on by businesses, the limit on damages for loss-only claims, the two-year period to bring the action, the carve-out for claims about negligently designed or manufactured computer products, and the statute's own definitions of "damage," "loss," and "exceeds authorized access."

This document is distinct from this corpus's existing California Comprehensive Computer Data Access and Fraud Act -- Demand Letter Information Sheet, which addresses the separate California civil cause of action in Penal Code section 502(e) -- a different statute with its own elements, remedies, and three-year limitations period. Conduct can potentially be examined under either or both statutes, but this document addresses only the federal CFAA civil remedy. This document is also distinct from this corpus's trade secret documents (including the DTSA and UTSA materials), which address trade secret misappropriation specifically; the CFAA civil remedy instead turns on unauthorized access to, or damage involving, a computer, regardless of whether a trade secret is involved.

Regarding Acme, Inc.'s internal customer database and CRM system and the conduct Acme, Inc. attributes to John Smith Manufacturing -- described as On March 3, 2026, the respondent appeared outside the petitioner’s home and yelled threats for several minutes before leaving., with loss or damage described as approximately $18,000 in forensic investigation and system restoration costs after a former employee accessed the company's file server after resignation -- this sheet sets out the statutory framework the law provides. It does not determine whether that conduct violates section 1030, whether a civil action under section 1030(g) would succeed, or what Acme, Inc. should do in response.

THE SECTION 1030(G) PRIVATE CIVIL ACTION
Section 1030(g) gives a private civil remedy to any person who suffers damage or loss by reason of a violation of section 1030. That person may bring a civil action against the violator to obtain compensatory damages and injunctive relief or other equitable relief.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Any person who suffers damage or loss by reason of a violation of this section may maintain a civil action against the violator to obtain compensatory damages and injunctive relief or other equitable relief."
  — 18 U.S.C. § 1030(g) (Cornell LII text), Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, private civil action (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/1030)
  Known gap: This is the statute's own text, quoted from 18 U.S.C. section 1030(g), used as evidence of the existence and general shape of the civil remedy -- not a claim that any specific access or conduct actually violated section 1030, and not a claim that any specific person suffered damage or loss as the statute defines those terms. The statute does not itself list which subsections of section 1030(a) can support a civil action; a civil action is available only for conduct that separately satisfies section 1030's substantive prohibitions and the qualifying-factor requirement addressed in the next clause. No case law on how courts have applied this remedy in practice was researched or is cited in this clause.

A CIVIL ACTION REQUIRES ONE OF FIVE STATUTORY FACTORS
Section 1030(g) does not allow a civil action for every violation of section 1030. A civil action may be brought only if the conduct involves one of five factors set out in a separate subsection, subclauses (I) through (V) of section 1030(c)(4)(A)(i): an aggregate loss of at least $5,000 in a one-year period; modification or impairment of medical examination, diagnosis, treatment, or care; physical injury to any person; a threat to public health or safety; or damage to a computer used by or for a United States government entity in furtherance of the administration of justice, national defense, or national security. (A sixth factor in that same subsection -- damage affecting ten or more protected computers in a one-year period -- is defined elsewhere in subsection (c)(4)(A)(i) but is not separately quoted here.)

  "(I), (II), (III), (IV), or (V) of subsection (c)(4)(A)(i)."
  — 18 U.S.C. § 1030(g) (Cornell LII text), Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, qualifying-factor requirement (part 2) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/1030)

That footnote number is an editorial annotation, not part of the substantive statutory text, so it is excluded from both quoted fragments rather than being quoted mid-sentence. No case law on how courts apply any of these factors was researched or is cited in this clause.

THE $5,000 AGGREGATE-LOSS FACTOR
The first of the qualifying factors under section 1030(c)(4)(A)(i) -- the one most often relied on in civil suits between businesses -- is loss to one or more persons during any one-year period aggregating at least $5,000 in value. For an investigation, prosecution, or other proceeding brought by the United States only, that aggregate loss can also include loss from a related course of conduct affecting one or more other protected computers.

  — 18 U.S.C. § 1030(c)(4)(A)(i)(I) (Cornell LII text), Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, $5,000 aggregate-loss factor (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/1030)
  Known gap: This is the statute's own text, quoted from 18 U.S.C. section 1030(c)(4)(A)(i)(I), used as evidence of the dollar threshold and the one-year aggregation period that subclause describes -- not a claim that any specific loss actually reaches $5,000 or that it was incurred within a single one-year period. Section 1030(e)(11) defines "loss" (quoted in a separate clause of this document); this clause does not itself restate that definition or address how a court would calculate whether a particular set of costs adds up to $5,000. The related-course-of-conduct aggregation language applies only to proceedings the United States brings, not to a private civil action; this clause does not address whether or how a private plaintiff could aggregate losses across multiple incidents or victims.

DAMAGES LIMITED TO ECONOMIC DAMAGES FOR LOSS-ONLY CLAIMS
Where the only qualifying factor for the civil action is the $5,000 aggregate-loss factor described above, section 1030(g) limits the damages available to economic damages. Damages for a violation involving only conduct described in subsection (c)(4)(A)(i)(I) are limited to economic damages.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Damages for a violation involving only conduct described in subsection (c)(4)(A)(i)(I) are limited to economic damages."
  — 18 U.S.C. § 1030(g) (Cornell LII text), Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, economic-damages limitation (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/1030)
  Known gap: This is the statute's own text, quoted from 18 U.S.C. section 1030(g), used as evidence that this damages limitation exists and of which claims it applies to -- not a claim about what dollar amount of economic damages any specific claim could support. The statute does not define "economic damages" in section 1030 itself; this clause does not supply or verify any definition of that term from another source. This limitation applies only when the $5,000 loss factor is the sole qualifying factor; a claim that also involves one of the other factors listed in section 1030(c)(4)(A)(i) (for example, physical injury or a threat to public health or safety) is not subject to this particular limitation, though this clause does not independently verify what broader damages might be available in that situation.

TWO-YEAR PERIOD TO BRING A CIVIL ACTION
A civil action under section 1030(g) may not be brought unless it is begun within two years of the date of the act complained of, or the date of the discovery of the damage, whichever comes into play under the statute's own terms.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "No action may be brought under this subsection unless such action is begun within 2 years of the date of the act complained of or the date of the discovery of the damage."
  — 18 U.S.C. § 1030(g) (Cornell LII text), Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, two-year limitations period (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/1030)
  Known gap: This is the statute's own text, quoted from 18 U.S.C. section 1030(g) -- not a claim about when any specific act occurred or was discovered, and not a claim about whether any tolling doctrine might extend or suspend this two-year period in a specific case. This two-year federal period is shorter than the three-year period this corpus's existing California Comprehensive Computer Data Access and Fraud Act information sheet describes for the separate state civil action under Penal Code section 502(e)(5); a claim time-barred under one statute is not necessarily time-barred under the other, since they are separate statutes with separate limitations periods.

NO CIVIL CLAIM FOR NEGLIGENT DESIGN OR MANUFACTURE OF COMPUTER PRODUCTS
Section 1030(g) does not allow a civil action for the negligent design or manufacture of computer hardware, computer software, or firmware. No action may be brought under this subsection for the negligent design or manufacture of computer hardware, computer software, or firmware.

The statute does not define "negligent design or manufacture" for purposes of this carve-out, and this clause does not address how this provision interacts with product-liability law outside of section 1030, or with claims that combine a section 1030 violation with a separate negligent-design theory.

STATUTORY DEFINITION OF "DAMAGE"
Section 1030 defines "damage" for purposes of the entire section, including the civil remedy in subsection (g). The term "damage" means any impairment to the integrity or availability of data, a program, a system, or information.

STATUTORY DEFINITION OF "LOSS"
Section 1030 also defines "loss" for purposes of the entire section, including the $5,000 aggregate-loss factor described above. The term "loss" means any reasonable cost to any victim, including the cost of responding to an offense, conducting a damage assessment, and restoring the data, program, system, or information to its condition prior to the offense, and any revenue lost, cost incurred, or other consequential damages incurred because of interruption of service.

STATUTORY DEFINITION OF "EXCEEDS AUTHORIZED ACCESS"
Several of section 1030's prohibitions, including ones commonly invoked in civil suits over employees or contractors who misuse computer access they were given, turn on whether a person "exceeds authorized access."
